newsitem.title: ECUADOR: RTRS-Ecuador aims to lure gold miners.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Ecuador aims to lure gold miners.

text.p: Ecuador is studying a new mining law to lure foreign investment and exploit the mountainous country's untapped gold potential, government and industry officials said.

The new law, which mining experts say could be in place by the end of the year, would replace legislation from 1991 and may include new tax incentives. But current royalties of three percent will probably stay in place.
"We need mining policies similar to those that Chile and Peru have," said Poli Guzm n, head of the Ecuadoran Mining Chamber. He said that current laws are not deterring trafficking in mining areas.

Most output is from informal, outdated operations, which evade government royalties. According to Jaime Jarrin, consultant to the National Mining Direction (Dinami), the state should have received $4.5 million in 1995, instead of the $230,000 it actually got.
The government estimates that Ecuadoran gold output will hit 569,000 ounces this year, and rise to 675,000 ounces in 1997 and 810,000 ounces in 1998. Gold production was 499,035 ounces last year.

According to government geological studies, Ecuador's biggest gold reserves lie in the El Oro province district of Portovelo Zaruma and in the Ponce Enriquez district of Azuay province. These two zones contribute 70 percent of current gold output.
Geologists say that the Cordillera del C ndor border district over which Ecuador fought a brief jungle war with Peru in 1995 also contains reserves of the precious metal.

"Many geological studies and experts in the subject agree that our country offers great mining possibilities. Even though the exploration investment necessary for them to be converted in mining reserves which could feasibly be exploited are lacking," Jarrin said in a report.

Mining companies are spending about $15 million a year exploring in Ecuador, according to industry sources. Companies including Canada's TVX Gold, Anglo-Australian giant RTZ-CRA and South Africa's Gencor already have prospects.
Ecuador should also prepare an inventory of its mining reserves and prospects, said Zoilo Angulo, head of the state-owned Mining and Geology Development and Investigation Corporation (Codigem).
